questions.question: Why is BCrypt a better choice for passwords than a fast hash such as plain SHA-256?
options: It is deliberately slow and uses a random salt, which makes guessing attacks expensive
It can be reversed when a user forgets the password
It does not need a database
questions.explanation: The salt and adjustable cost make each guess costly, and no hash can be turned back into the password.

questions.question: Where does Spring's BCrypt hash keep its salt?
questions.explanation: The version, cost and salt are part of the hash string, so matches() can read them without extra storage.

questions.question: Two members register with the same password using BCryptPasswordEncoder. What does hashA.equals(hashB) return?
options: true, because the passwords are equal
false, because each hash has its own random salt
questions.explanation: encode() adds a new random salt every call, so equal passwords give different hashes.

questions.question: A login method runs encoder.encode(typed).equals(savedHash) and never succeeds. What is the fix?
options: Store the password in plain text
questions.explanation: A fresh encode uses a new salt, so it never equals the saved hash. matches() reuses the saved salt.

questions.question: Every BCrypt login fails after a developer stores hashes in a varchar(50) column. What is the likely cause?
options: BCrypt hashes are 60 characters, so the column cuts them
The cost is set too high
questions.explanation: A truncated hash can never match, so the column must hold at least 60 characters.
